The same two anchors are centered on that cell: the tall one, (2, 0, 4, 6), and the square one, (2, 2, 4, 4). Anchors are labeled by Faster R-CNN's rule, as on the page.
Which anchor is trained toward the line, and what is its target $t_w$?

choices.explain: The line overlaps each anchor in a strip 2 wide and 1 high, an area of 2. The square anchor covers 4, so its IoU is 2 / (4 + 6 − 2) = 0.25. The tall one covers 12, so its IoU is 2 / (12 + 6 − 2) = 0.125. Both are below 0.3, but every object gets its best anchor, and that is the square one. In center form the line is 6 wide and the anchor 2, so t_w = log(6 / 2) = 1.099. Its other targets are t_x = 0, t_y = (2.5 − 3) / 2 = −0.25 and t_h = log(1 / 2) = −0.693.

The square anchor is the right one, but the width target is the logarithm of the ratio of widths, log(6 / 2) = 1.099, not the difference over the anchor's width. The difference would make three times as wide and a third as wide unequal in size, 2 against −0.67, where the logarithm gives 1.099 and −1.099.

The tall anchor was the vertical line's, but it covers 12 square units to meet this line in only 2. Its IoU is 2 / 16 = 0.125, half the square anchor's 0.25, so the square anchor is the line's best and the tall one is background.

choices.text: Neither: both IoUs fall below 0.3, so both anchors are background
choices.explain: Both IoUs are below 0.3, but the rule also gives every object its best anchor, whatever that anchor's IoU. Without it this line would have no anchor, and the detector would never be trained to find it. The square anchor, at 0.25, is the best.

theory.title: What NMS Does to Average Precision
overview: A line detector is scored on four 6 × 6 test images, each holding one line. Boxes are (left, top, right, bottom) in pixels, and image 1 is the running example:

setup.p: Use the rules of the page. Non-maximum suppression, when it is used, runs on each image with threshold 0.5. A predicted box is a true positive when its IoU with the true box of its image is above the scoring threshold and no more confident box has already matched that true box. Otherwise it is a false positive. For the average precision (AP), go down all the boxes in order of confidence, and each time a true positive appears note the precision of the boxes so far. AP is the sum of those precisions divided by the number of true boxes, 4, so a true box that is never found adds 0. Since recall rises in steps of 1/4, the sum measures the region below the precision-recall curve.

prompt.p: What is the AP at IoU 0.5 without non-maximum suppression?

answer.p: All six boxes are scored: D, A, F, C, B, E. C overlaps its true box well enough, but D has already matched it, so C is a false positive, and so is B after A. The true positives sit at ranks 1, 2 and 6:
The two duplicates did not lower recall. They lowered the precision at which E was found, from 3/4 to 3/6, because both outrank it.

prompt.p: What is the AP at IoU 0.75 without non-maximum suppression? Compare it with the AP at IoU 0.75 after non-maximum suppression.

answer.p: At 0.75 only the boxes with IoU 0.833, A and C, can be true positives. Without non-maximum suppression the order is D, A, F, C, B, E. D fails the threshold, so it matches nothing and is a false positive. A is a true positive at rank 2, precision 1/2. C is next for image 2, and since D did not match the true box, C does, a true positive at rank 4, precision 2/4. So

After non-maximum suppression the order is D, A, F, E. Only A is a true positive, at rank 2, and $\text{AP} = (1/2) / 4 = 0.125$, half as much. Non-maximum suppression keeps the most confident box, not the best placed one, and in image 2 it threw away C, the only box good enough at this threshold.

prompt.p: A teammate says that duplicate boxes cannot lower AP, since they never lower recall, and that non-maximum suppression can only raise it. Say when each claim fails, using the parts above.

answer.p: Duplicates lower AP exactly when they outrank a true positive, because each one adds a false positive to the precision of every true positive found after it. In Part 2, C and B sit above E and take E's precision from 3/4 to 3/6. Give C and B confidences below 0.60 and the order becomes D, A, F, E, B, C: the true positives keep the precisions 1, 1 and 3/4, and AP is 0.6875 again. A duplicate ranked below every true positive costs nothing.

Non-maximum suppression removes those false positives, but it chooses by confidence, so it can remove a better placed box and keep a worse one. At IoU 0.5 it helps, 0.6875 against 0.625, because both boxes it kept still match. At 0.75 it halves the AP, as Part 3 found. The COCO benchmark's average over the thresholds 0.5, 0.55, ..., 0.95 comes out at 0.3125 with non-maximum suppression and 0.325 without, so on these four images it loses overall. The remedy is a confidence that tracks how well a box is placed, so that the box kept is also the best placed one.
